commits.message:
Serve /submit only once a submit check worker has loaded (#885)

Before, the /submit handler was published while its check workers were
still loading, so requests at startup waited in the pool holding ingress
slots. The load-harness stack test, which sends at once, got 21 of 85
requests refused "503 HTTP ingress capacity is full" (run 42422865297
shard 3, reproduced locally with the same counts).

The pool gains whenReady(timeoutMs). The node waits on it before serving
/submit, bounded by the 30 s worker start bound; a pool that loads no
worker in time is served anyway, as after a crash, so startup never
hangs on it. The peer-node test helper waits the same way.

The stack test predated #886 and #887: it expected every well-formed tx
admitted. It now asserts each kind's outcome: valid and missing-input
202 (the ledger view stays cold here), bad CBOR, bad signature and low
fee 400, double spend 409 E_INPUT_SPENT.

Tests: submit-ingress-load.stack, submit-check-pool (8, new whenReady
case), submit-request-handler, l2-peer-routes: 23 passed.

Replace a rerun Aiken shard's stale report instead of adding beside it

The shard report upload runs even when the shard fails, so a failed
attempt leaves its report in the run. A partial rerun (rerun failed
jobs) uploaded the passing report under the same name, and the
collector's aiken-shard-report-* download read the stale one: run
42420884846 attempt 2 had shard 3 pass 4,056 checks with 0 errors, yet
the collector saw attempt 1's 1.7 KB report and failed with "compiler
did not exit successfully". overwrite: true makes the rerun replace it.

Judge a trusted proxy's socket address once, not per request (#885)

Over TCP, httpClientIdentity normalized the socket peer address, parsed
it to bytes and walked the HTTP_TRUSTED_PROXY_PEERS ranges on every
request. Behind a proxy nearly every request comes from the same peer.
The verdict on the last peer address is now kept, one slot per proxy
list, so a repeat costs one string compare. The verdict depends only on
the address and the list, so the slot changes no answer. A stream of
different peers only replaces the slot, so memory stays fixed. A missing
list now falls back to one shared empty list rather than a fresh array,
which had also defeated the parsed-range cache.

The HTTP_SOCKET_PATH branch (production nginx over a Unix socket) is
unchanged; it never reads a socket peer.

Warm microbenchmark of httpClientIdentity for a trusted proxy and 4,096
named clients: 388 ns -> 36 ns per call.

Tests: listen-http-ingress, listen-http-rate-limit,
listen-http-rate-buckets, listen-http-liveness,
listen-http-submit-bounds, listen-public-http, submit-request-handler
and l2-peer-routes passed (100 passed). This change is meant to keep
behavior the same, so no new test.

M2 (main-thread us per request, one run each, HEAD and this change
interleaved per rate, before -> after). Every delta is inside the
+/-10 us run-to-run noise:
- 1,000 req/s: 321 -> 310, all admitted.
- 3,000 req/s: 204.7 -> 200.7, all 30,000 admitted.
- 5,000 req/s: 194.2 -> 193.4. Both runs still refuse 586 and 186 of
  50,000 for ingress capacity, with p50 latency about 112 ms.

Admit a checked /submit tx without an Effect fiber (#885)

The raw /submit handler handed each checked tx to
admitCheckedTransaction through Runtime.runCallback. That forked a fiber
per request to run a dozen Effect steps that are all synchronous.
makeCheckedTransactionsAdmitter now captures the services admission reads
once, when the handler is built, and returns a plain function. The
handler calls it and answers in the same tick.

The admitter keeps the order: duplicate lookup, then the shed by submit
source (the backlog reservation), then the writer's stall and pending
bounds, then the input claims, then registration. The refusals and
metrics are the same. The gauge reservation, the shed counter, the
spendable view and a refused tx's release still run as Effects, through
the captured runtime's runSync. The writer's durable work stays
asynchronous.

AdmissionWriterService.admitBatch is now a plain synchronous call. It
registers the batch and offers the items with Queue.unsafeOffer. The lane
queues are unbounded and shut down only after `accepting` turns false, so
every registered item is taken. admit stays an Effect over it.
admitCheckedTransaction(s) wrap the admitter for Effect callers such as
/peer/txs.

A defect thrown by the admitter answers 500 internal_error, as a failed
fiber did.

Tests: submit-request-handler, submit-check-workers, database.test,
l2-peer-admission, l2-peer-routes, l2-peer-forwarder, admission-shedding,
admission-input-claims, admission-writer-batch, admission-writer,
admission-writer-collector, admission-writer-pipeline, submit-fail-fast
and startup-http-server passed (174 passed). This change is meant to keep
behavior the same, so no new test.

M2 (main-thread us per request, one run each, before -> after):
- 1,000 req/s: 339 -> 322.
- 3,000 req/s: 218.7 -> 203.3, at 0.674 -> 0.572 cores. The measured run
  went from 16 refusals to all 30,000 admitted.
- 5,000 req/s: 210 -> 192.8, at 0.976 -> 0.893 cores. 566 of 50,000 were
  still refused for ingress capacity. p50 latency was 92 ms.

Move the admission hand-off out of the submit checks module (#885)

This is a pure move. The checked-transaction admission code moves out of
transaction-admission.ts into a new checked-transaction-admission.ts:
AdmissionCandidate, AdmissionRefusal, admitCheckedTransaction(s) and the
batch entry types. transaction-admission.ts keeps the stateless checks.
At 493 lines it had no room for the synchronous admitter the next commit
adds.

The /submit handler and /peer/txs import from the new module. The
writer's doc comment points there.

Evidence: verify-pure-move.mjs confirms that the 14 top-level declarations
are unchanged across the two files. tsc, eslint and prettier are clean.
submit-request-handler, admission-writer-batch and l2-peer-routes passed
(15 passed).

Warm the M2 bench up and size its check pool from the measured check (#885)

The M2 bench now runs a warm-up first, on a corpus of its own:
SUBMIT_MAIN_THREAD_WARMUP_SECONDS seconds (default 3) at the measured rate.
The CPU sample and the numbers leave it out. The measured run must still
be admitted in full. The bench prints its row and each run's outcome mix
before that assertion, so a failing run still shows its cost and whether
its refusals followed a client burst. maxLagRequests, the most requests
the client sent at once after falling behind, is now in the row.

By default the check pool is sized from the submit check cost the bench
measures, so the workers run at about half load at the offered rate.
Since #886 the check costs about 445 us per tx, not 74. Two workers top
out near 4,400 tx/s, so at 3,000 and 5,000 req/s the pool queued bodies
until the ingress refused them for capacity. That measured the workers,
not the main thread. SUBMIT_MAIN_THREAD_WORKERS still sets the pool size
explicitly.

M2 at this commit (main-thread us per request; 10 s measured run, 10 %
keep-alive, 329 B txs):
- 1,000 req/s, 2 workers: 339 us, all 10,000 admitted.
- 3,000 req/s, 3 workers: 218.7 us at 0.674 cores. 16 of 30,000 were
  refused for ingress capacity, after a client burst of 76 requests.
  The warm-up took 104 refusals.
- 5,000 req/s, 6 workers: 210 us. The main thread is saturated at 0.976
  cores, p50 latency is 122 ms, the client lagged by up to 3,975 requests,
  and 563 of 50,000 were refused for ingress capacity.

The warm-up removes the cold-start refusals: the warm-up runs take them
(104 at 3,000 req/s). It does not make 5,000 req/s pass. At this
commit the main thread cannot serve 5,000 req/s.

Delete the stale MAX_SUBMIT_QUEUE_SIZE line from .env.example (#886)

The node no longer reads MAX_SUBMIT_QUEUE_SIZE: the durable admission
backlog bounds (MAX_DURABLE_ADMISSION_BACKLOG and its byte bound) replaced
the in-memory submit queue. The example file still set it to 10000 with
no comment. No other file mentions it (git grep is empty after this
change).

Tests: none. The line is a config example that nothing reads.

Run Phase A on the ingress check's own decode (#886)

The submit check decoded each tx once for itself, then handed the bytes to
validatePhaseASingle, which decoded them again. Its two canonical item
scans decoded them twice more, and its consensus check decoded them once
more. At 1/2 that duplicate work was most of the check's 0.46 ms.

midgard-validation: validatePhaseASingle is now split into its own scans
and decode followed by validatePhaseAAfterDecode, the shared rest
(tx id binding, consensus profile and bounds, network, fee, the input,
interval, signer, signature, script and ex-unit rules, the candidate). The
new export validatePhaseASingleDecoded(queuedTx, {nativeTx, submittedTx},
config) takes a normal tx decoded by
decodeMidgardSubmittedNativeTxFromCanonicalCbor. It runs the same two
scans over the decoded field preimages, runs validateMidgardConsensusTx on
the decoded tx, then calls the same shared rest. It throws for a forced
tx. The scans are now canonicalFieldOrderFaultInPreimages and
oversizedOutputIndexInPreimage, and the byte-taking forms wrap them, so
the bytes path runs the same steps in the same order with the same
catches.

Why the decoded path matches: deriveMidgardTxFieldPreimages(bytes,
"normal") takes its preimages from decodeMidgardNativeTxFullFromCanonicalCbor
(bytes), the same decode the caller ran, so the scans see the same nine
preimages. The rest of that function (version check, consistency check,
compact encode and decode round trip) only repeats checks a successful
decode has already passed. validateMidgardConsensusTxCbor is that decode
followed by validateMidgardConsensusTx with the same byte length.

midgard-node: checkSubmittedTransaction passes its own decode to
statelessRefusal, which now calls validatePhaseASingleDecoded. The
function and its module keep their names and places.

Tests:
- New tests/phase-a.decoded-entry.test.ts compares the two paths with
  toStrictEqual (verdict, code, detail, phase and subject, or the whole
  validated candidate). It runs under a zero fee floor and under the
  ingress floor (1/byte + 2,000). The corpus is 21 hand-built txs plus
  every normal row of the ORDER, NATIVE, ASSET_ENTRY and
  resolve-inputs FULL/PLAIN emission-order corpora. The hand-built txs:
  valid, bad signature, no witness, wrong network, start after end, no
  inputs, descending spend inputs, descending reference inputs,
  descending address witnesses, repeated input, repeated witness,
  spend/reference overlap, oversized output, unwitnessed required
  signer, aux data, is_valid false, wrong queued id.
- The test asserts the corpus reaches acceptance and each verdict the
  decoded path computes on its own: the order fault at fields 0, 1 and
  7, the width fault at field 2, E_AUX_DATA_FORBIDDEN and
  E_IS_VALID_FALSE_FORBIDDEN. It also asserts E_INVALID_SIGNATURE,
  E_MIN_FEE, E_NETWORK_ID_MISMATCH and E_TX_HASH_MISMATCH. One row,
  e_refusal_malformed_native_witness, does not decode; a caller refuses
  it before Phase A.
- Red: three mutations of the decoded path each fail it. Skipping the
  order scan fails "descending spend inputs", returning a null
  consensus violation fails "auxiliary data hash", and skipping the
  width scan fails "output past the canonical width bound".
- Green: 28 midgard-validation suites that reach Phase A pass (443
  tests), including phase-a, canonical-field-order, the emission-order
  machine rows, the ed25519 suites, reject-subject* and
  forced-native-first-fault. midgard-node submitted-tx-check,
  submit-fail-fast, submit-ingress-load, l2-peer-admission and
  l2-peer-routes pass (42 tests).
- eslint, prettier --check and tsc --noEmit are clean for both
  packages. The midgard-validation dist is rebuilt and the doctor's
  dist preflight passes.

bench:submit-check, check variant, median ms per tx, one process per
shape. The before side is this tree with HEAD's transaction-admission.ts.

  shape   before   after
  1/2     0.456    0.190
  4/4     0.777    0.439

At 16/16 the tx carries 16 vkeys, so signatures set a floor of about

Docs: the design doc's D6 text and capacity row, and the docs-site Phase A
page, now describe the decoded entry point and give the new figures.

Move Phase A's script and ex-unit rules into their own module (#886)

Pure move, ahead of the change that gives Phase A an entry point for an
already-decoded tx. That change takes phase-a.validate-phase-asingle.ts
past the package's 500-line eslint max-lines limit.

Four top-level declarations move from phase-a.validate-phase-asingle.ts
to the new phase-a.validate-script-rules.ts: validateWitnessScripts,
validateRequiredObservers, validateScriptEvaluationPreconditions and
validateDeclaredExUnits. They are the static script rules Phase A runs
after the signatures. All four become exports of the new module. Phase A
imports them from it and drops the imports only they used. Nothing else
changes.

verify-pure-move.mjs --before HEAD:.../phase-a.validate-phase-asingle.ts
--after both files:
"Pure move confirmed: 9 top-level declarations in 1 before file(s) at
79be16fb1f0d; 9 in 2 after file(s)".

Gates: midgard-validation tsc --noEmit, eslint and prettier --check are
clean. Seven Phase A suites pass (132 tests): phase-a,
carried-plutus-script-decoding, value-accounting,
spent-plutus-script-source.admission, forced-native-first-fault,
reject-subject.malformed-native and validity-interval-upper-bound.

Refuse junk a stateless Phase A check catches before admission (#886)

checkSubmittedTransaction, the check /submit and /peer/txs run before
durable admission, now runs validatePhaseASingle with the validation
pool's settings (network id from NETWORK, MIN_FEE_A and MIN_FEE_B) and
refuses with 400 and Phase A's own code when Phase A returns
E_INVALID_SIGNATURE, E_MIN_FEE or E_NETWORK_ID_MISMATCH. It then runs
Phase B's expiry check against the wall clock 60 s back
(SUBMIT_EXPIRY_CLOCK_MARGIN_MS) and refuses a passed validity interval
with E_VALIDITY_INTERVAL_MISMATCH. Every refusal is one validation itself
makes, so ingress and validation cannot disagree; Phase A's other
verdicts are left to the validation pool. The check stays a pure
function of the bytes, the rules (network, fee rule, L1 slot mapping from
Lucid) and the clock, with no database access, so lane D can move it into
the worker pool. A signature verifier that is not initialised answers 503
with Retry-After, never a verdict.

/peer/txs runs the same checks (design D6 skips only the stateful check
for peers); a refused tx counts in "refused".

The database fixtures' native txs carried a signature over the Cardano
body hash, not the Midgard tx id, so Phase A refused them; they are now
re-signed over the Midgard id with a fixed key. The load tx builder takes
a body network id and a validity end, and the load corpus test now
expects bad-signature and low-fee junk refused at ingress.

Docs: PUBLIC_HTTP.md, the docs-site server HTTP API page, the public
testnet parameters table, the design doc (D6 as built, measured check
cost) and the load harness README.

Tests: submit-fail-fast.test.ts (real /submit and /peer/txs, each junk
class refused with its code while Postgres refuses connections, nothing
stored) and the forged-witness case in l2-peer-admission.test.ts failed
before the change (3 failed: 202 for junk, peer bodies admitted) and pass
after. Green after: submitted-tx-check, submit-ingress-load,
submit-fail-fast, l2-peer-admission (34 passed); database.test,
admission-writer, local-mutation-job-abandonment (145 passed);
l2-peer-routes, l2-peer-forwarder, l2-peer-scheduler-emulator,
admission-shedding, listen-http-submit-bounds, listen-http-rate-limit,
listen-admission-auth, startup-http, startup-http-server,
startup-http-cli-provider (90 passed).

Cost (bench:submit-check, one shape per process, median ms per tx):
1/2 0.074 -> 0.461, 4/4 0.113 -> 0.760, 16/16 0.310 -> 2.096. Phase A
alone is 0.41 ms at 1/2; one Ed25519 verify is 55 us.

Resolution on the submit check workers (#885): /submit's check runs in
the worker pool, so the rules travel to the workers as plain data.
acquireSubmitCheckPool reads submittedTxRules once on the main thread (the
network and fee rule from NodeConfig, the slot mapping from Lucid) and
puts them in SubmissionCheckConfig with the size cap. Each worker passes
its own Date.now(), read once per batch, as the clock. No Lucid runs in a
worker. A 503 verdict leaves the raw handler with Retry-After 5 and the
body {error: "Signature verification is unavailable"}, which is what the
Effect handler gave. It is counted under its own refusal reason,
signature_verifier_unavailable. The shed 503 from #883 already came out
of the raw handler with the same status, body and Retry-After.

A worker now posts ready only after ledgerEd25519SignatureReady resolves.
libsodium initialises per isolate. Before this change a fresh worker
answered its first bodies 503 "Signature verification is unavailable"
until the verifier came up. That readiness wait is bounded at 10 s, under
the pool's 30 s start bound. If libsodium fails or times out, the worker
throws an uncaught error. The pool then stops it, answers its waiting
bodies with the retryable "unavailable" 503 and starts a fresh worker with
backoff. Nothing waits on it without a bound. The design doc's D6 says
this.

The fixtures merge lane F's re-signing over the Midgard tx id
(signedOverMidgardId) with lane D's worker-pool router. The pool is keyed
by its config, rules included, and the rules come from submittedTxRules
under the test's Lucid, or the Preprod slot mapping when the test has
none. The raw handler's test harness and the M2 bench carry explicit
rules.

Red before the worker readiness wait: with every conflict resolved and
the worker posting ready at load, the gate set had 28 failures in 15
files (171 passed). All of them were the first body a fresh worker
checked answering 503 instead of 202/409, plus one startup test that
retried into its 420 s timeout. Green after: submit-request-handler,
submit-check-pool and submit-fail-fast passed (15 of 15).

The #887 case "releases a rejected tx's claims" relied on a tx with a
forged signature being admitted and then rejected by validation. Phase A
at ingress now refuses that tx with 400. The case now uses a transfer of
funding plus an output the ledger never held. Ingress admits it because
the ledger view is still cold, and it claims funding. Validation rejects
it, so the claims are released and the second spender is admitted. The
case went from red (400, expected 202) to green.

Green after, with everything resolved: submit-request-handler,
submit-check-pool and submit-fail-fast passed 15 of 15. admission-shedding,
submitted-tx-check, admission-writer-batch, l2-peer-admission,
l2-peer-routes, l2-peer-forwarder, submit-ingress-load, database.test,
submit-check-workers, startup-http-server and admission-writer passed
183. admission-input-claims passed 9 of 9 after the case was rewritten.

Check /submit bodies on a dedicated worker thread pool (#885)

The envelope decode and the submission check now run on a pool of
worker_threads apart from the validation pool, so the main thread only
reads the body, hands it over and admits the verdict. The worker imports
checkSubmissionBody from commands/http/submission-check.ts, the module the
handler ran inline; the check takes its config as an argument and stays a
pure function of the bytes, the config and the clock.

- SUBMIT_INGRESS_WORKER_POOL_SIZE (default 2) sizes the pool.
  SUBMIT_INGRESS_WORKER_QUEUE (default 256) and
  SUBMIT_INGRESS_MAX_IN_FLIGHT_BYTES bound the slots a request holds from
  the body read to the verdict; a full queue answers 503 with Retry-After
  and keeps the connection. /submit no longer takes the
  SUBMIT_INGRESS_MAX_CONCURRENCY permits, which now size the peer pool only.
- The bodies of one tick go to each worker as one message with their
  buffers transferred. An accepted tx comes back as one transferred buffer
  of tx id, full hash and canonical bytes, plus outrefs, fee and size, so
  the main thread neither decodes nor hashes.
- A worker takes bodies once it says it has loaded the check; bodies
  posted while every worker is loading wait for it. A worker that exits,
  throws, does not load within 30 s or leaves a batch unanswered for 10 s is
  terminated, the requests it held get 503 "Submit check is unavailable;
  retry later" (reason submit_check_unavailable), and it is replaced after
  a backoff of 50 ms doubling to 5 s.

Tests, all through real workers and a real HTTP server:
- submit-check-pool: the production worker's verdicts deep-equal the check
  run inline on a corpus covering acceptance and every refusal kind; one
  message per tick; queue and byte bounds; a hung batch is answered and its
  worker replaced; a slow-loading worker is waited for with no batch timer;
  a worker that never loads is stopped; close answers held bodies.
- submit-check-workers: a full queue answers 503 keep-alive; the handler
  answers from the worker's result (a canned worker accepts junk); a worker
  killed mid-load (process.exit and an uncaught throw, inside 200
  concurrent requests) answers its requests 503 and ingress admits again
  with both workers back.

Red before: with the check run inline in the handler and no respawn, 2 of
9 handler tests failed (the canned-worker and crash tests); with no respawn
alone, 2 of 14 failed (pool replacement, crash test); against the pool
before the load handshake, 2 of 7 pool tests failed; routing bodies to
workers that have not loaded failed the slow-load test (unavailable, not
checked).

Green after: database.test, l2-peer-routes, l2-peer-admission,
submit-request-handler, submit-check-pool, submit-check-workers,
startup-http-server, admission-writer 149/149; l2-peer-forwarder,
l2-peer-scheduler-emulator, validation-retry-config, node-instance-lock,
local-mutation-job-abandonment, http-read-byte-budget and the handler file
63/63; listen-startup validation-worker-readiness and
ledger-signature-verifier fault files in a 32/32 run.

M2 (bench:submit-main-thread, 1,000 req/s for 10 s, two workers): 335 us of
main thread per request at 10 % keep-alive and 288 us all keep-alive,
against 506 us and 467 us with the check on the main thread (#881).

The test fixture posts each submission from a loopback address of its own,
since a request now waits for a worker and the ingress holds a client to
four in flight. The junk-flood test now checks that every sampled line is
the flood's one reason and allows two lines a second: one loaded run
logged 5 lines over a 2 s flood.

Shed anonymous submits at 80 % of a larger admission backlog (#883)

The admission layer now picks the backlog bounds by submit source before it
reserves a slot: /submit (native) may fill 80 % of the row and byte bounds,
/peer/txs the full bounds. The refusal comes from the in-memory gauges, so a
shed answers 503 with Retry-After and does no database work, and it holds for
whichever HTTP handler calls admitCheckedTransactions. The 503 body names the
per-source limit as maxBacklog or maxBacklogBytes.

The default backlog rises from 10,000 rows and one DA payload of bytes to
300,000 rows (60 s at 5,000 TPS) and 1 KiB per row (307,200,000 bytes). Both
are provisional until the M1 gate (#877). Readiness stays at 95 % of the row
bound (285,000), above the 240,000-row anonymous share. Raising the bound
costs no node memory: the gauges are counters, the pending set keeps its own
bounds and the recent-id ring is fixed; the backlog lives in Postgres.

Docs: PUBLIC_HTTP.md, README load-harness limits, .env.example, the docs-site
HTTP API page, the public testnet parameters table and open items, and D5 in
the ingress design.

Tests:
- New admission-shedding.test.ts drives real HTTP into a shard node: at 85 %
  of the rows (17/20) with the database refusing connections, /submit gets
  503 Retry-After 5; after reconnecting a peer offer is admitted; at 85 % of
  the bytes /submit is shed and a peer is admitted, and at 100 % the peer is
  refused. Red before the change (2 failed: expected 202 to be 503), green
  after (2 passed).
- The admission database tests that sized their bounds for /submit at 100 %
  now size them for the 80 % share; the default-value case for the old byte
  default is removed. TxAdmissionsDB 34 passed.
- validation-retry-config, admission-backlog-gauge, admission-writer-batch,
  l2-peer-routes, l2-peer-admission, l2-peer-forwarder, admission-shedding:
  37 passed.

Admit a /peer/txs body in one writer submission (#882)

The admission writer gains admitBatch: one synchronous registration runs the
duplicate check, the pending-set bounds and the registration for every request
in order, so a request repeating an earlier one in the same batch answers as
its duplicate or conflict, and one refusal stops no other. admit is now a
batch of one. The pending-set bound checks move to
admission-writer.pending-bounds.ts, which keeps the writer module under the
500-line limit.

transaction-admission.ts gains admitCheckedTransactions, the batch form of the
hand-off: it reserves a backlog slot per tx, makes one admitBatch call and
releases every reservation the writer did not take. admitCheckedTransaction
keeps its signature and delegates to it. /peer/txs checks every tx, admits the
passing ones in one call and answers once. A capacity refusal on any tx still
answers 503, so the forwarder backs off and catches up by inventory. Txs
before or after it in the body may already be admitted.

M3 (peer ingest on one lane, real route, real writer, test Postgres, 327 B
txs, 20 sequential signed bodies, rate limit off, two runs after the change):
before 5,212 tx/s on 500-tx bodies and 8,162 on full 888-tx bodies; after
6,701-8,209 and 9,265-9,820. A full body is answered in 78-87 ms at the median
and under 0.2 s at worst. The receiver no longer bounds a lane. The peer rate
class does (4 req/s, about 3,500 tx/s at this tx size), which clears the
1,000 TPS target. So the body bound stays one largest tx, and the forwarder
request timeout drops from 30 s to 10 s. The design doc records the
reasoning.

Tests: tests/admission-writer-batch.test.ts covers the batch semantics against
the real statement while the table is locked. It failed before the change
(TypeError: writer.admitBatch is not a function) and passes after. The new
500-tx route test in l2-peer-routes.test.ts passes, and it passed before the
change too, because the ack from memory (#874) had already removed the
per-tx commit wait. The full-backlog stub in the database admissions tests
now also refuses admitBatch. Writer, peer, forwarder, database admissions
and startup suites all pass.

Cherry-picked onto lane D (raw /submit handler, #885 worker pool, #887
input claims). Conflict resolution: the writer's per-request register() also
runs the request's claimInputs after the pending-set bounds, as lane E's
inline admit did; admitCheckedTransactions keeps lane E's claim taking per
reserved tx (claims released with the backlog slot on any non-new answer or
an unwritten settle) and reads the spendable view once per batch, right
before admitBatch; /peer/txs counts an AdmissionInputSpentError (which a
peer never gets) as a conflict, not a capacity refusal. The raw handler's
test harness stub writer gains admitBatch.

Serve POST /submit from a raw Node handler with sampled refusal logs (#881)

POST /submit no longer goes through the Effect router. The startup listener
now owns the one Node request listener: once the node publishes, POST /submit
goes to makeSubmitRequestHandler (commands/http/submit.ts) and every other
request to the Effect application, as before.

The raw handler runs the same ingress checks every route runs. The gate in
listen-http-ingress.ts is now a plain function (admitHttpRequest) that both
withHttpIngress and the raw handler call, with one shared controller per
node configuration, so identity, target, route, Content-Length (411/413),
media type, the hashed limiter and per-client in-flight answer with the same
codes, bodies and keep-alive rules. The submit ingress permits are plain
counts shared with the peer route's withSubmitIngressPermit. The handler then
reads the declared body, runs checkSubmissionBody (envelope decode plus
checkSubmittedTransaction, a pure function a worker can load) and hands the
checked tx to admitCheckedTransaction; admission refusals map to the same
HTTP answers as before.

Refusals increment submit_refusal_count{reason} and log only the first
refusal per reason per wall-clock second, with the count left unlogged. The
handler records one latency histogram (submit_handler_latency) and the
admitted counter (tx_count) with synchronous metric updates; the per-stage
Effect timers and submit_queue_offer_failure_count are gone, and the stress
script reads the refusal total instead. The Effect postSubmitHandler and
buildSubmitRouter are deleted; the admission fixture, the L2 peer test node
and the M2 bench serve the raw handler over real HTTP.

M2 (bench:submit-main-thread, 1,000 req/s, 10 % keep-alive, writer stubbed):
688 us of main thread per request on the Effect handler before this change,
506 us after (467 us with every connection kept alive). The design doc's
capacity rows, PUBLIC_HTTP.md and the server HTTP API page say so.

Tests: the new submit-request-handler suite (6) covers the ingress refusals,
check refusals, a rate refusal on a kept connection, startup dispatch, and a
2,000-request junk flood at about 1,000/s that must log at most one line per
second; with sampling disabled it fails (2,000 lines, limit 3) and passes with
it. The existing ingress, startup, admission, database and L2 peer suites pass
unchanged in what they assert (335 tests in 31 files).

Resubmit a lost tx once and resolve a spent-input refusal from its status (#888)

The node now acknowledges /submit from memory (design D9). A 202 means
accepted, not yet stored, so the node can lose a tx after acknowledging
it, and /tx-status then answers 404 not_found. The node also refuses a
second spender of a claimed input with 409 E_INPUT_SPENT (design D6,
#887), and that tx may be the client's own already-held tx. Before this
change the provider reported the lost tx as not_found forever, and it
failed the refusal as an error.

Lost txs:
- MidgardNodeProvider remembers the bytes of each tx it got acknowledged,
  per process, capped at 1,024 with the oldest dropped first. It forgets
  a tx once it settles.
- When /tx-status turns not_found for a remembered tx, getTxStatus
  resubmits it exactly once and reads the status again. This covers
  status(), awaitStatus() and awaitTx on that provider.
- A resubmission that fails retryably (503, transport) is tried again on
  the next read.

Spent-input refusals:
- On a 409 E_INPUT_SPENT, submitTx reads /tx-status. If the node holds
  the tx, the submit resolves to that status as a duplicate (httpStatus
  200). Statuses past acceptance map to accepted.
- Otherwise the 409 stays a non-retryable error.

A 503 on submit stays retryable.

Tests: tests/provider.lost-tx.test.ts runs the provider against a real
node:http server double:
- 202 then lost: exactly one resubmit;
- no resubmit for a foreign tx;
- 503 on the resubmit, then a retry;
- a spent-input refusal for an accepted tx and for a queued tx resolves;
- a spent-input refusal for a tx the node does not hold fails;
- a 503 stays retryable.
Against the previous provider 4/7 failed and 3 passed; the 3 that passed
guard behavior the provider already had. Now 7/7 pass, and with
provider.test.ts and submit-status.test.ts 45/45 pass.
